nameStory: The rough wood aster gets its name from the texture of its leaves, which feel distinctly sandpapery or rough to the touch - like fine-grit sandpaper! This roughness comes from tiny hairs and bumps on the leaf surface that you can actually feel when you run your finger across them. It's one of the most reliable ways to identify this woodland wildflower.
description: Rough wood aster is a low-growing perennial wildflower that brightens up wet woodlands and boggy areas in late summer and fall. It produces delicate daisy-like flowers with pale blue-violet petals (called rays) surrounding bright yellow centers, creating a lovely contrast against the darker woodland backdrop. The plant typically stays fairly short and spreads by underground stems, forming small colonies in suitable habitats. Like other asters, it belongs to the sunflower family and is an important late-season nectar source for butterflies and other pollinators.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Feel the leaves - they have a distinctly rough, sandpapery texture that immediately sets them apart from smooth-leaved relatives. The roughness is caused by tiny hairs and bumps you can actually feel with your fingertips.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pale blue-violet petals (usually 8-15 rays) surround bright golden-yellow centers, blooming from late summer into early fall when many other wildflowers have finished.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Stays relatively low and compact compared to other asters, often forming small patches through underground spreading rather than growing as tall individual plants.

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Almost always found in consistently moist to wet soils - look for it near streams, in boggy areas, wet ditches, or other places that stay damp even in dry weather.

habitat: Rough wood aster thrives in consistently wet soils across a variety of New England habitats, from sphagnum bogs and fens to stream banks and roadside ditches. It prefers areas that stay moist year-round, often growing alongside sedges, ferns, and other moisture-loving plants. You'll rarely find it in dry upland woods - if the soil isn't soggy or at least consistently damp, look elsewhere for this species.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the weather warms, showing the characteristic rough-textured leaves that make identification possible even before flowering.
seasonality.summer: Foliage develops fully through the summer months, but flowers don't typically appear until late in the season.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming time! The pale blue-violet flowers with bright yellow centers appear from late summer through early fall, often lasting into October.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, leaving little trace above ground until spring growth begins again.

funFact: Despite being called a 'wood' aster, rough wood aster is actually more of a wetland specialist - it's happiest with its feet constantly wet, making it one of the few asters you're likely to find growing right in a bog or swampy area where most other wildflowers would drown!
confusionNotes: The rough, sandpapery leaf texture is your best friend here - run your fingers across the leaves and you'll immediately know if you've found rough wood aster. Other blue-purple fall asters in the region have smooth or only slightly hairy leaves that feel much different to the touch.
contextualKnowledge: This species was recently moved from the genus Aster to Eurybia, so you might see it listed in older field guides as Aster radula. Many botanists and field guides are still catching up with this name change, which happened as scientists better understood the relationships between different aster species.
compareHints: Among its wood aster relatives, rough wood aster is the wetland specialist with the distinctive sandpapery leaves. White wood aster prefers drier woods and has smooth white flowers, while large-leaved aster has much bigger, heart-shaped leaves and also grows in drier conditions. The rough leaf texture and wet habitat preference make this species quite distinctive within the Eurybia genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its wood aster relatives, white wood aster is the only one with the distinctive serpentine stem pattern.

Among the wood asters, large-leaved aster is easily distinguished by its oversized basal leaves - white wood aster has much smaller, narrow leaves, while Schreber's wood aster has more elongated leaves.
Purple wood aster stands out from its wood aster relatives by having the most vibrant purple flowers - white wood aster is obviously white, while large-leaved aster has much bigger, broader leaves.
Among wood asters, Schreber's is distinguished by its extremely rough leaf texture - much rougher than White Wood Aster's smooth leaves or Large-leaved Aster's softer, fuzzy leaves.

Among its wood aster relatives, slender aster stands out for its narrow, upright form while white wood aster spreads wider with heart-shaped leaves, and large-leaved aster has distinctively broad foliage.
